newsitem.title: India: India, Bangladesh sign key water-sharing pact.
newsitem.headline: India, Bangladesh sign key water-sharing pact.

text.p: India and Bangladesh signed a new treaty to share water from the Ganges River on Thursday, which the leaders hailed as a stepping stone to improved relations between the South Asian neighbours.
Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda and Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina of Bangladesh signed the 30-year agreement on the last day of Hasina's three-day visit to the Indian capital.
The treaty removes the greatest irritant in relations between the two nations.
"We are confident that this treaty would be a landmark in our bilateral relations," Deve Gowda said in a statement to parliament after signing the treaty in Hyderabad House palace.
"The key merit of this formula is that it shares available waters on a basis which is fair and equitable."

Bangladesh and a large portion of northern India depend on water from the Ganges. The level of water can vary dramatically, flooding large areas during the monsoon or falling to dangerously low levels during the January-June dry period.
Deve Gowda said at a banquet on Wednesday evening that the treaty opened a new chapter in bilateral relations.
"Let this agreement on the sharing of the Ganges waters be a stepping stone for greater cooperation between Bangladesh and India," Hasina said.

In 1977, the two nations signed an agreement to let Bangladesh take a guaranteed minimum of 34,000 cubic feet per second (cusecs) between October and June every year. But the guarantee was dropped in a new six-year accord signed in 1982.
The decades-old water dispute worsened after India built the Farakka Barrage in 1974, curbing the flow of the Ganges, which irrigates India before flowing into Bangladesh.

A senior Indian Foreign Ministry official said that under the new treaty, if the water flow at the barrage near the two countries' border was below 70,000 cusecs, the nations would split the water evenly.
If the flow was between 70,000 and 75,000 cusecs, then Bangladesh would receive 35,000 cusecs, the official said. Above 75,000 cusecs, 40,000 cusecs would be guaranteed to India.
Deve Gowda told parliament the accord would be reviewed every five years.

An opposition leader, Atal Behari Vajpayee of Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), said he welcomed improvement in India's relations with Bangladesh but added, "We can talk about the accord only after reading (the details of) the statement."
The agreement was expected to give a political boost to Hasina, who like Deve Gowda, assumed power in June following general elections.

At the signing ceremony, Deve Gowda and Hasina were flanked by their foreign and water resources ministers. The communist chief minister of India's West Bengal state, Jyoti Basu, who played a key role in negotiating the treaty, was also present.
West Bengal state, which borders Bangladesh, and its capital Calcutta, are heavily dependent on the Ganges.
Bangladesh had charged that India holds back water during the annual January-June dry season and releases excessive quantities during monsoon rains, causing flooding.
